entities.summary:
Argentina, officially the Argentine Republic, is the second-largest country in South America (2,780,400 km²) and fourth-largest in the world by area. Located in the southern cone of South America, it spans from subtropical forests in the north to glacial Patagonia and Tierra del Fuego in the south. With 46 million people, Argentina is the most economically significant Spanish-speaking country in South America.

Indigenous peoples inhabited the region for millennia before Spanish colonization (1516). The Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata (1776) made Buenos Aires a major colonial capital. Independence was declared on July 9, 1816, making Argentina one of the first independent republics in Latin America. The late 19th and early 20th centuries brought massive European immigration — six million immigrants from Italy, Spain, Britain, and Eastern Europe between 1880 and 1930 — creating a uniquely cosmopolitan culture that makes Argentina demographically distinct from other South American nations.

Argentina's modern history is defined by alternating civilian and military governments, economic crises, and extraordinary cultural output. The Perón era (1946–1955, 1973–1976) created a populist political tradition (Peronism) that still structures Argentine politics. The Dirty War military dictatorship (1976–1983) killed 30,000 people. Argentina's economic collapse (2001) remains the largest sovereign debt default in history. Yet it also produced one of Latin America's most vibrant literary, cinematic, and musical cultures — home of the tango, Jorge Luis Borges, and Astor Piazzolla.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Argentina's declaration of independence in 1816 led to the formation of a major republic in Latin America, influencing regional politics and shaping the continent's future. Its strategic location facilitated European immigration, contributing to its economic significance.
